problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have successfully solved the problem. The final answer is \boxed{4048}.

**b. Method Sketch:**  
1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   - Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares forms a permutation matrix: there exists a bijection \(\pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (with \(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\pi(i))\).

2. **Decomposition into left and right parts.**  
   - For each row define  
     \[
     L_i:=\pi(i)-1\qquad(\text{cells left of the uncovered square}),\qquad 
     R_i:=n-\pi(i)\qquad(\text{cells right of the uncovered square}).
     \]
   - The multiset \(\{L_i\}\) equals \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\); the same holds for \(\{R_i\}\).
   - Any rectangular tile cannot contain an uncovered square, hence each tile lies entirely in the left part \(\{(i,j):1\le j\le L_i\}\) or entirely in the right part \(\{(i,j):\pi(i)+1\le j\le n\}\).

3. **Lemma (left side).**  
   - For each \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) let \(i_k\) be the unique row with \(L_{i_k}=k\).  
   - The cell \((i_k,k)\) is the right‑most cell of row \(i_k\) in the left part.  
   - **Claim.** Any rectangle covering \((i_k,k)\) cannot contain any other cell \((i_{k'},k')\) with \(k'\neq k\).  
     *Proof.* If a rectangle \(T\) covers \((i_k,k)\) and its column interval is \([c_1,c_2]\), then \(c_2\le L_{i_k}=k\) (otherwise row \(i_k\) would need a column beyond its left part). Since column \(k\) belongs to \(T\), we have \(c_2=k\); thus the column interval of \(T\) is \([c_1,k]\).  
     For any row \(i\) with \(L_i<k\) the column \(k\) does not exist, so such a row cannot belong to \(T\).  
     For any row \(i\) with \(L_i>k\) the special cell of that row is \((i,L_i)\) with column \(>k\), which is not in the column interval of \(T\). Hence \(T\) contains at most the single special cell \((i_k,k)\). ∎  
   - Since the \(n-1\) cells \((i_k,k)\) are pairwise distinct, at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed to cover the left part.

4. **Right side.**  
   - Reflect the board horizontally (replace column \(j\) by column \(n+1-j\)). The right part becomes a left part of the reflected board, so the same argument yields that at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed for the right part.

5. **Lower bound.**  
   - Any tiling uses at least \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) tiles.

6. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   - Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\). Then \(L_i=i-1\) and \(R_i=n-i\).  
   - For each row \(i=2,\dots ,n\) place a **left tile** covering the cells \((i,1),\dots ,(i,i-1)\) (a \(1\times (i-1)\) rectangle).  
   - For each row \(i=1,\dots ,n-1\) place a **right tile** covering the cells \((i,i+1),\dots ,(i,n)\) (a \(1\times (n-i)\) rectangle).  
   - All tiles are disjoint, they cover every cell except the diagonal cells \((i,i)\); each row and each column contains exactly one uncovered cell.  
   - The number of tiles is \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\).

7. **Conclusion.**  
   - The lower bound \(2n-2\) is attainable, therefore it is the minimum.  
   - For \(n=2025\) the minimum number of tiles is \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\).

Hence the answer is \boxed{4048}.

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there exists a bijection  
\[
\pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]
such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\pi(i))\).

For each row \(i\) define  

\[
L_i:=\pi(i)-1\qquad\text{(number of squares left of the uncovered one)},
\]
\[
R_i:=n-\pi(i)\qquad\text{(number of squares right of the uncovered one)} .
\]

Since \(\pi\) is a permutation, the multiset \(\{L_i\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}\) equals \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\); the same holds for \(\{R_i\}\).

The **left part** of the board is  

\[
\mathcal L:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;1\le j\le L_i\},
\]

and the **right part** is  

\[
\mathcal R:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;\pi(i)+1\le j\le n\}.
\]

A rectangular tile cannot contain an uncovered square, therefore every tile is completely contained either in \(\mathcal L\) or in \(\mathcal R\).  
We treat the two parts separately.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1 (left part)

For each integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n-1\) there is a unique row
\(i_k\) such that \(L_{i_k}=k\).  
The cell \((i_k,k)\) is the right‑most cell of row \(i_k\) belonging to \(\mathcal L\).

*Claim.* Any rectangle \(T\subseteq\mathcal L\) that covers \((i_k,k)\) cannot contain any other cell \((i_{k'},k')\) with \(k'\neq k\).

*Proof.*  
Let the column interval of \(T\) be \([c_1,c_2]\) with \(c_1\le k\le c_2\).  
Since row \(i_k\) contains columns only up to \(L_{i_k}=k\), we must have \(c_2\le k\).  
Because column \(k\) belongs to \(T\), we obtain \(c_2=k\); thus the column interval of \(T\) is \([c_1,k]\).

If a row \(i\) satisfies \(L_i<k\), column \(k\) does not belong to that row, so \(i\) cannot be part of \(T\).  
If a row \(i\) satisfies \(L_i>k\), its special cell \((i,L_i)\) lies in column \(L_i>k\), which is not contained in the column interval \([c_1,k]\); consequently \((i,L_i)\) is not in \(T\).  

Hence \(T\) contains at most the single special cell \((i_k,k)\). ∎

There are exactly \(n-1\) distinct cells \((i_k,k)\) (one for each \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\)).  
Since each rectangle of a tiling can contain at most one of them, any tiling of \(\mathcal L\) uses at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 2 (right part)

Reflect the board horizontally by the map \((i,j)\mapsto(i,n+1-j)\).  
Under this reflection the right part \(\mathcal R\) becomes the left part of the reflected board, and the numbers \(\{R_i\}\) become the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  
Applying Lemma 1 to the reflected board shows that any tiling of \(\mathcal R\) also requires at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lower bound for the whole board

Every tile lies wholly in \(\mathcal L\) or wholly in \(\mathcal R\); therefore any tiling of the whole board uses at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Construction attaining the bound

Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\) for all \(i\).  
Then \(L_i=i-1\) and \(R_i=n-i\).

*Left tiles.* For each row \(i=2,\dots ,n\) place a rectangle covering the cells
\[
(i,1),(i,2),\dots ,(i,i-1),
\]
i.e. a \(1\times(i-1)\) rectangle anchored at the left border.

*Right tiles.* For each row \(i=1,\dots ,n-1\) place a rectangle covering the cells
\[
(i,i+1),(i,i+2),\dots ,(i,n),
\]
i.e. a \(1\times(n-i)\) rectangle anchored at the right border.

All these rectangles are pairwise disjoint; they cover every cell of the board except the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).  
Consequently each row and each column contains exactly one uncovered square (the diagonal one).  

The number of tiles used is  

\[
\underbrace{(n-1)}_{\text{left tiles}}+\underbrace{(n-1)}_{\text{right tiles}}=2n-2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Conclusion

The lower bound \(2n-2\) is achievable, hence it is the minimum possible number of tiles.  
For \(n=2025\),

\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}=2\cdot2025-2=4048 .
\]

Thus the answer is \boxed{4048}.
